# werk — instructions for the agent

This repository builds its own design tool. Use the tool while you build it.

## Keep the map current, every turn

When the conversation settles something, append it to the log **in the same turn**:

```bash
node src/cli.ts add <id> --title "..." --why "..." --parent <id> --status <s> --who <w>
node src/cli.ts link <from> <to> --type depends_on
node src/cli.ts status <id> decided
node src/cli.ts reopen <id>
```

Do not batch this up for later. The map is the record of what the conversation established.
The transcript is not.

## After a structural map change, ask whether the diagram should move too

`.werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid` is a second, hand-authored description of the product
— see #vi-sysdiag-grain and #vi-sysdiag-derive. It does not update itself, and nothing in the
log keeps it in sync.

Only a **decided** card may justify diagram content. At the end of any turn where you added,
retitled, relinked, or changed the decided-status of a card that names a real running part of
the system — not a note, not a why-only edit — spawn two subagents in order, in the same turn.
A status change is exactly the trigger, not an exception to it: a card becoming decided can
add content, and a decided card being reopened removes its standing to justify any — see
#vi-sysdiag-agents.

1. `sysdiag-scout` — tell it exactly what changed: the ids, the operations, the before/after
   titles or edges. It reads the current diagram and reports whether it still matches, and if
   not, the precise content-section change needed.
2. If it reports a change, `sysdiag-updater` — hand it that report verbatim. It edits the
   `.wgrid` file and rebuilds with `bun src/gridsys/build.ts` until the tile grammar (R1–R6,
   see `src/gridsys/check.ts`) passes with 0 errors.

Most turns end at step 1 with `NO CHANGE NEEDED`: most decided cards are about the map itself,
not about a drawable part of the product. Do not force a diagram edit to justify running these.

## Eryk refers to cards by id

An id looks like `#werk-excerpt`. When he pastes `re #<id> "<title>": ...`, he typed that in
the map. Run `node src/cli.ts inbox` to read the whole thread, then reply with
`node src/cli.ts say <id> "..."` so the answer lands on the card, not only in the terminal.

## Record `depends_on` at the moment you create a card

A single-hop model check recovers only 6% to 11% of an invalidation chain. There is no way
to reconstruct these edges later. If a card is true only because another card is true, write
the edge now, or staleness propagation is dead and the map rots into a pretty outline.

`refines` is where a card **sits**. `depends_on` is what a card **needs**. They are different
graphs over the same nodes. That is the whole point.

## Record a rejected option the moment you weigh it

When a decision comes from real contrast in conversation — you named an alternative, gave a
reason, and rejected it — add that alternative as its own `option` node with `--why_not`, and
link it `alternative_to` the decided card, in the same turn:

```bash
node src/cli.ts add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
node src/cli.ts link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to
```

If you skip this, the card is indistinguishable later from one decided with no contrast at
all — the `unchallenged` marker cannot tell "no option was weighed" from "an option was
weighed but never written down." Both #ro-unchal and #vi-backend were corrected after the
fact because of this. Do not create a third case.

## Say so when a card you just made comes out stale

A new card inherits a reopen from anywhere upstream of its `depends_on` targets, however many
hops away. It turns red the moment you create it, and Eryk sees the red mark before he sees
your message. Say it yourself in the same turn: name the origin, and say the card was written
with that correction already in hand.

Run `node src/cli.ts show <id>` after you create a card. It prints the whole trace —

---
name: wayfinder
description: Plan a huge chunk of work — more than one agent session can hold — as a shared map of decision tickets on your issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride _inside_ the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A real named goal, written as one or two lines on the map body. Its *type* is constrained: \"the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to.\" So usually the planning artifact — \"a spec for a tool doing X, ready to hand off\" — not \"the tool doing X\". Not always: the skill allows \"a change made in place like a data-structure migration\", and an effort can carry execution into the map through its Notes.
